Saddam Hussein. The dictator of Iraq from nineteen seventy-nine to two thousand three, ruling through the Ba'athist Party with authoritarian brutality. Hussein rose through the Ba'athist Party, becoming vice chairman in nineteen sixty-eight and consolidating power over the next decade before formally assuming the presidency in nineteen seventy-nine. In nineteen eighty, he launched the Iran-Iraq War, invading his neighbor over border disputes and regional hegemony. The conflict became a stalemate lasting eight bloody years and killing roughly one million people. Hussein used chemical weapons against Iran and against Kurdish civilians in northern Iraq, representing one of the worst instances of chemical warfare since World War I. In nineteen ninety, he annexed Kuwait, triggering the Gulf War the following year, in which a U.S.-led coalition expelled Iraqi forces and humiliated his military. Throughout his rule, he maintained a brutal secret police and military apparatus that suppressed Shiite and Kurdish minorities through massacres and displacement. Under UN sanctions and weapons inspections, he remained in power through the nineteen-nineties, defying international pressure. The two thousand three U.S. invasion finally removed him. He was captured in December two thousand three, tried for crimes against humanity, and executed by the Iraqi government in December two thousand six. As his regional rival during the Iran-Iraq War, Ayatollah Khomeini had opposed him fiercely.
